entities.summary:
IBM (International Business Machines Corporation), founded in Armonk, New York in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company and renamed IBM in 1924 under Thomas J. Watson Sr., is the technology company most responsible for creating the modern computing industry — producing the System/360 (1964, the first family of mutually compatible computers), the IBM PC (1981, which defined personal computing standards), the Deep Blue chess computer (1997, which defeated Garry Kasparov), and Watson AI (2011, which defeated Jeopardy! champions). IBM has received more US patents than any other company for 28 consecutive years.

Thomas Watson Sr.'s IBM transformed punch card tabulation (used in the 1890 US Census) into a worldwide computing services business. The System/360 (1964) — a $5 billion development program, the largest private industrial investment in history at the time — created the first family of mutually compatible computers from mainframes to small systems, establishing the hardware compatibility standard that all subsequent computing inherited. IBM's 1981 PC decision — using open architecture and Microsoft's MS-DOS — inadvertently created the PC clone market that allowed competitors to undermine IBM's hardware dominance.

IBM's transformation from hardware manufacturer to services and consulting company (1990s-2000s) under Louis Gerstner's turnaround saved IBM from bankruptcy after the PC clone market collapse. The 2019 Red Hat acquisition ($34 billion) repositioned IBM in hybrid cloud and Linux. IBM Watson AI — beating Jeopardy! champions in 2011 — pioneered natural language AI for enterprise applications. IBM's quantum computing research (IBM Quantum Network) is a leading civilian quantum computing program.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: IBM's System/360 (which created hardware compatibility standards inherited by all computing) and the IBM PC's open architecture (which inadvertently created Microsoft's dominance) make IBM the company that most shaped modern computing's technical architecture — twice creating industry standards that outgrew IBM itself.
